report.releaseDate: 24 Nov 2026 (ECA/GCI "Online Gaming 2023–2025: Illegal Gambling in EU27 Europe"; wire release 25 Nov 2026)
report.currency: EUR (tables in € billions unless stated; ~USD alongside at EUR/USD 1.095)
report.verdict: The ECA-commissioned GCI study sizes the EU27 online betting-and-gaming marketplace at €128.0bn (~$140.2bn) GGR in 2025, of which only €36.5bn (~$40.0bn, 28%) sits with locally licensed operators and €91.6bn (~$100.3bn, 72%) with operators lacking the national licence required — a cumulative €224.8bn (~$246.2bn) "illegal" take and €56.3bn (~$61.6bn) of forgone tax over 2023–25. The regulated base is corroborated by EGBA/H2 (EU27+UK online €47.9bn in 2024, implying ~€36–37bn ex-UK) and is growing high-single digits, but the black-market figure is 5–8x the competing Euromat/Regulus (€12bn net, ~25%) and H2 (~€18bn, ~27%) estimates and should be treated as an upper bound. For an operator the EU remains 27 separate, expensive (avg €1.1m initial fee, 24% avg GGR tax) national regimes with no passporting; the actionable opportunities are the markets re-regulating in 2026–28 (Finland, Austria, Ireland) and the better-channelised Nordic and Southern European markets, not an "EU-wide" play.
summary: **Market structure — one online marketplace, two industries.** GCI's monitoring for the European Casino Association (ECA) puts EU27 online GGR (sports betting, casino and poker incl. crypto; lotteries, DFS, prediction markets and land-based excluded) at €78.4bn (~$85.8bn) in 2023, €114.3bn (~$125.2bn) in 2024 and €128.0bn (~$140.2bn) in 2025; over three years the marketplace totalled €320.8bn (~$351.3bn), split €95.9bn (~$105.0bn, 30%) locally licensed vs €224.8bn (~$246.2bn, 70%) unlicensed.

**Regulated base is growing, but losing share.** Licensed online GGR rose from €25.8bn (~$28.3bn) in 2023 to €33.6bn (~$36.8bn) in 2024 (+30%) and €36.5bn (~$40.0bn) in 2025 (+8.6%); its share of the online marketplace fell from 33% to 29% to 28%. Of the €49.7bn (~$54.4bn) increase in annual GGR over 2023–25, unlicensed operators captured €39.0bn (~$42.7bn), or 78%.

**Illegal growth is decelerating, which the headline obscures.** Unlicensed GGR grew +53% in 2024 (€52.6bn→€80.6bn) but only +13.6% in 2025 (→€91.6bn, ~$100.3bn); the 2026–28 trajectory depends on whether that deceleration is enforcement-driven or a calendar effect (2025 had no major international football tournament).

**The headline black-market number is contested by 5–8x.** Euromat's Regulus/Helios study (Sept 2026; 28 markets = EU27 ex-Malta/Luxembourg + UK, Serbia, Montenegro) puts illegal online NET revenue at ~€12bn (~$13.1bn), ~25% of the sector and tripled since 2019 (~18% CAGR); H2 Gambling Capital is reported at ~€18bn (~$19.7bn), ~27%. The regulated base is consistent across all three; the disagreement is entirely about the unlicensed denominator and GCI's audience-based 'value-per-visit' method, which counts every transacting domain (mirrors included).

**Regulated base corroborated by EGBA/H2.** EGBA's Key Figures 2025 (H2 data, EU27+UK, includes grey-market online) show total European GGR of €123.4bn (~$135.1bn) in 2024 (+5%), online €47.9bn (~$52.5bn, 39% share, +12% from €42.9bn in 2023) and land-based €75.5bn (~$82.7bn). Stripping the UK's ~€11bn online implies an EU27 online figure of ~€36–37bn — in line with GCI's regulated €33.6–36.5bn and IMGL's €35–40bn 2025 estimate. EGBA/H2 project online at €51.1bn (~$56.0bn, 40%) in 2025 and €66.8bn (~$73.1bn, 45%) by 2029 (6.9% CAGR).

**Casino dominates online demand; sports is better channelised.** GCI's 2025 product split is 70% casino / 30% sports for the total online marketplace; regulated GGR is 41% sports / 59% casino while illegal GGR is 25% / 75%. Derived values: regulated sports ~€15.0bn (~$16.4bn) vs illegal ~€22.9bn (~$25.1bn) (legal channelisation ~40%); regulated casino ~€21.5bn (~$23.5bn) vs illegal ~€68.7bn (~$75.2bn) (~24%). H2 puts EU27+UK licensed/grey online casino at €21.5bn and online sports at €13.7bn in 2024.

**Regional leak is worst in Eastern Europe, best in the Nordics.** 2025 unlicensed share: Eastern 81% (€30.7bn of €37.7bn), Western 74% (€36.9bn of €50.1bn — the largest region), Southern 60% (€17.1bn of €28.4bn), Northern 58% (€6.9bn of €11.9bn). Regulated GGR grew fastest in Southern Europe (+12%) and slowest in Western Europe (+6.5%) in 2025.

**Licensing regime — 27 national licences, no passporting.** There is no EU gambling directive; each member state licenses and taxes separately under CJEU-sanctioned national competence, and the ECA itself asks for 'national licences, European cooperation' rather than an EU regulator. GCI's 2025 benchmark: average initial multi-product licence fee €1.1m (~$1.2m) in the EU27 vs €8,183 (~$9.0k) at transnational licensors (Anjouan, Curaçao, Isle of Man, Malta); recurring €355k (~$389k) vs €33k (~$36k); EU regulators also typically demand bank guarantees/share capital.

**Tax regime — GGR-based in most states, averaging 24%.** GCI's average gaming tax across GGR-regime member states is 24.0% (vs 2.3% transnational), with corporate tax averaging 18.9% vs 8.8%. Turnover-based betting taxes persist in a minority (e.g. Germany, Poland, Ireland [not re-verified this session]); recent increases include the Netherlands (to 34.2% in 2025, 37.8% from 2026) and Sweden (22% from July 2024) [background, unverified in-session]. A BGC-commissioned H2GC study forecasts an 11ppt channelisation decline in the Netherlands after the 2025 rise and the KSA itself forecast a 9% fall in 2025 tax receipts.

**Tax 'loss' figures are internally inconsistent.** ECA quotes €22.9bn (~$25.1bn) forgone in 2025 and €56.3bn (~$61.6bn) over three years (≈25% of illegal GGR), while GCI's September 2026 Campaign for Fairer Gambling edition quotes €22.0bn (~$24.1bn) at a 24% average rate on the same €91.6bn base. Both are gross hypotheticals that assume full substitution into licensed play at headline rates.

**Operator landscape.** EGBA's nine members (bet365, Entain, Betsson, Evoke, FDJ United, Flutter, LeoVegas, Super Technologies/Superbet, Tipico) generated €18.0bn (~$19.7bn) online GGR in 2025 (+34%, from €13.5bn), hold 401 online licences across 22 jurisdictions and claim ~30% of Europe's online GGR — equivalent to ~49% of GCI's EU27 regulated figure. On the illegal side GCI counted 6,238 transacting destinations in 2025 (4,921 in 2023; 6,220 in 2024) and 17,501 affiliates (21,106 in 2023); Euromat finds 25 brands drive ~64% of black-market traffic. A consolidated EU-wide licensed-operator count does not exist (n/a).

**Payments are the chosen enforcement lever.** The ECA argues that if banks, card schemes and PSPs stopped settling with unlicensed operators 'their business model would break'; GCI describes a compartmentalised 'triangle trade' (licensing, sites/apps and content in different jurisdictions) that gives unlicensed operators banking continuity and payment resilience, with crypto play included in its estimates. Payment-method mix is not disclosed (n/a).

**Advertising and platform exposure is overwhelmingly illegal.** GCI's audience-exposure metric attributes 91% of gambling content actively engaged with by EU27 consumers in 2025 to unlicensed operators (85% in 2023); 121m Europeans saw online gambling content in 2025, 88m from unlicensed sources. Cloaked-ad brokers (over half EU-based) sell into all 27 states with 85% approval rates and promise 1,100+ monthly first-time depositors; slots content on Kick is 'blocked' in six states but effective only in Greece; 19% of Kick's outbound traffic went to Stake during 2026 World Cup peaks.

**Responsible-gambling rules are being marketed against.** Unlicensed sites advertise 'casinos not on CRUKS' (NL) and 'not on ROFUS' (DK), targeting self-excluded players; Euromat counts 'significant advertising restrictions' in 46% of the 28 markets studied (incl. BE, BG, HR, CY, DE, IT, LV, LT, NL, PL, RO, ES), product bans in 14% (CY, FR, DE, PL) and consumer-price taxation in 29% (AT, HR, DE, IE, PL, PT) as the structural drivers of leakage.

**Political direction — enforcement, not harmonisation.** The ECA's July 2026 European Parliament roundtable (hosted by MEP Lukas Mandl; Commission, AMLA, Eurojust and the Europol JPSG attending) coincided with the Commission's proposal to reform Europol's mandate; the ECA wants regulator–police–FIU information sharing and platform/app-store/search take-downs; Euromat calls for a European taskforce. Expect EU action through AML, Europol and platform rules rather than a gambling directive.

**Market-opening pipeline is real.** Finland moves from the Veikkaus monopoly to multi-operator licensing (go-live 2027), Austria's government approved a reform to open the online market on 25 Nov 2026 ahead of its 2027 licence expiry, and Ireland's new regulator published draft eligible-game lists for its licensing regime this week — three new licensed casino/betting markets inside 24 months.

**Event cadence matters.** GCI flags 2025 as a gap year; the 2026 World Cup generated 17.8bn qualifying (90s+) illegal stream views in Europe, 95% carrying unlicensed gambling ads, and the 2026 Champions League final 51.3m (93%). Over 80% of illegal sports streams in the EU27 carried unlicensed gambling ads in 2024–25.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** The licensed addressable pool is ~€36.5bn and compounding ~8–11% a year; entry costs ~€1m+ per market plus 20–40% GGR tax and rising compliance; the illegal competitor set is real in every state but its scale is contested. Prioritise (i) the 2026–28 openings (FI, AT, IE), (ii) Northern/Southern markets with 40%+ regulated share and GGR-based tax, and (iii) products where regulation does not structurally handicap the legal offer (avoid building a casino-led case in FR, PL, DE under current rules).

segments.name: Market size & channelisation (regulated vs illegal)
segments.headline: A €128bn online marketplace in which licensed operators hold 28% by GCI's count — but 73–75% by the Euromat and H2 methods; the regulated base (~€36.5bn) is the only number all sources agree on.
narrative: GCI's monitoring for the ECA covers the whole EU27 online marketplace for sports betting, casino and poker (crypto-denominated play included; lotteries, daily fantasy, prediction markets, sweepstakes, social casino and all land-based excluded). On that definition total GGR reached €128.0bn (~$140.2bn) in 2025 (the November release rounds to €128.1bn), up 12.0% from €114.3bn (~$125.2bn) in 2024 and 63% from €78.4bn (~$85.8bn) in 2023. Locally licensed operators earned €36.5bn (~$40.0bn) in 2025, up 8.6% after +30% in 2024, while operators without the national licence required earned €91.6bn (~$100.3bn), up 13.6% after +53% in 2024. Across the three years the split is €95.9bn (~$105.0bn) regulated against €224.8bn (~$246.2bn) unlicensed, i.e. 30/70 of a €320.8bn (~$351.3bn) marketplace, and illegal operators absorbed €39.0bn (~$42.7bn) of the €49.7bn (~$54.4bn) increase in annual GGR (78% of growth). GCI equates the 2025 illegal take to more than €250m (~$274m) a day and €6.24bn (~$6.8bn) a month across the period.

The regional pattern is sharp. Eastern Europe (BG, HR, CZ, HU, PL, RO, SK, SI) is 81% unlicensed — €30.7bn (~$33.6bn) of €37.7bn (~$41.3bn) — reflecting monopolies (Poland's online casino, Hungary, Slovenia) and turnover taxes; Western Europe (AT, BE, FR, DE, IE, LU, NL) is the largest region at €50.1bn (~$54.9bn) and 74% unlicensed, with illegal GGR having more than doubled in 2024 (+104.5%) before slowing to +15.7% in 2025 — consistent with France's online-casino prohibition, Germany's restrictive GlüStV and the Dutch tax rise; Southern Europe (CY, GR, MT, IT, PT, ES) is 60% unlicensed on €28.4bn (~$31.1bn) and delivered the fastest regulated growth (+12% to €11.3bn, ~$12.4bn); Northern Europe (DK, EE, FI, LV, LT, SE) is the best channelised at 42% regulated on €11.9bn (~$13.0bn). Illegal growth in 2025 was strongest in Southern (+22.1%) and Northern (+21.1%) Europe and weakest in Eastern Europe (+5.9%), where the market may be approaching saturation.

Corroboration is partial. EGBA/H2's Key Figures 2025 put online GGR for the EU27 plus the UK at €47.9bn (~$52.5bn) in 2024 (39% of €123.4bn, ~$135.1bn total), explicitly including 'white and grey' online activity; EGBA's 2023 country table shows UK online at €11.1bn (~$12.2bn), so the EU27 ex-UK online figure is roughly €36–37bn — consistent with GCI's €33.6bn regulated for 2024 and with IMGL's €35–40bn estimate for 2025. H2 data cited by the Dutch regulator's spring report shows the licensed EU online market growing 11% from 2024 to 2025. The regulated denominator is therefore robust to within a few billion euros. The unlicensed numerator is not: Euromat's Regulus/Helios study (Sept 2026) finds ~€12bn (~$13.1bn) of illegal NET revenue across 28 markets (EU27 ex-MT/LU plus UK, Serbia and Montenegro), ~25% of the sector, up ~3x since 2019 (≈18% CAGR), with shares up to 80% in the worst jurisdictions and France singled out as the largest illegal market; H2 is reported at ~€18bn (~$19.7bn) or ~27%. GCI's estimate is 5–8x these, driven by its audience-based 'value-per-visit' model, inclusion of crypto casinos, and counting of every active, transacting domain (mirrors and redirects separately). GCI itself concedes that 'assessment of large complex online marketplaces is limited by the availability and completeness of data'.

GCI's audience measures are its leading indicators. Population impact — the share of residents reached by gambling content — was 23.03% in 2025 (29.26% in Eastern Europe), with 16.76% reached by unlicensed operators: 121m Europeans saw online gambling content and 88m of them saw unlicensed content. Audience exposure — content actively interacted with — was 91% unlicensed (96% in Eastern Europe, 81% in Northern Europe), up from 85% in 2023, which GCI presents as an early-warning indicator of where future GGR will flow rather than a share measure.

Commercially, the implication for an operator is two-sided. The licensed pool is ~€36.5bn and compounding at 8–11% a year with casino the larger and faster product; EGBA's nine members alone grew 34% to €18.0bn (~$19.7bn) in 2025, which suggests scale incumbents are taking share inside the licensed pool even as the pool loses share to the unlicensed. Whether the unlicensed competitor set is €12bn or €92bn changes the pricing and bonus intensity you must plan for: in Eastern Europe and in product-restricted Western markets the practical competitor is an offshore crypto-friendly casino with no tax, no KYC friction and 3x advertising ROAS, and licensed economics have to be built on that assumption.

segments.name: Online sports betting
segments.headline: Sports is ~30% of EU27 online GGR and the better-channelised product (~40% licensed), but event-driven peaks — and the illegal streams that monetise them — are where unlicensed recruitment concentrates.
narrative: GCI's blended product split attributes 30% of the 2025 EU27 online marketplace to sports betting (32% in 2024), which on the €128.0bn total implies ~€37.9bn (~$41.5bn) of sports GGR [derived]. Within that, sports is 41% of regulated GGR (~€15.0bn, ~$16.4bn) but only 25% of illegal GGR (~€22.9bn, ~$25.1bn), giving a legal channelisation rate of roughly 40% — far better than casino's ~24%. The regulated sports share is highest in Western Europe (47%, reflecting France where licensed operators may offer only betting, horse racing and poker) and lowest in Northern Europe (37%); the illegal sports share is highest in Southern (31%) and Eastern (30%) Europe and lowest in Western Europe (20%), where the unlicensed offer is overwhelmingly casino.

The H2/EGBA series, which covers EU27 plus UK and includes grey-market online activity, puts online sports and events betting at €13.7bn (~$15.0bn) in 2024, up 11% from €12.3bn (~$13.5bn) in 2023 and 29% of online GGR, with €14.5bn (~$15.9bn) forecast for 2025 and a 6.9% CAGR to €19.2bn by 2029; online horse racing adds €2.5bn (~$2.7bn). The gap between H2's €13.7bn (which contains the UK's large betting market) and GCI's ~€36bn total sports (EU27 only) is the clearest single illustration of how much larger GCI's unlicensed count is than the industry-standard series.

National product mixes differ materially. EGBA's 2023 country data show sports leading online in Cyprus (74%) and Slovakia (64%), while France's €3.8bn (~$4.2bn) online market is betting- and poker-led because online casino is prohibited; Germany's licensed market is lottery- and betting-heavy (lottery 37% of online). Betting is also the product most often taxed on turnover rather than GGR — Germany (5.3% of stakes), Poland (12% of stakes) and Ireland (2% of stakes) [background, not re-verified this session] — which structurally compresses the legal price and is cited by Euromat as a driver of leakage in AT, HR, DE, IE, PL and PT.

Event cadence drives both legal and illegal volumes. GCI characterises 2025 as a gap year with no World Cup or European Championship, which is one plausible contributor to the deceleration of illegal growth to +13.6%. For the 2026 World Cup it counted 17.8bn qualifying (90-second-plus) illegal stream views across Europe, 95% of which carried advertising for gambling operators not licensed in the viewer's jurisdiction, and 51.3m for the 2026 Champions League final (93%); more than 80% of illegal sports streams viewed in the EU27 carried unlicensed gambling ads in both 2024 and 2025. During World Cup peaks 19% of outbound traffic from the Kick streaming platform went to Stake. The ECA frames illegal streaming as putting younger viewers 'one click away from a bet'.

For B2Tech the practical read is that sports betting is the lower-leakage, lower-regulatory-friction entry product across most of the EU27, that turnover-tax markets require a pricing model built around margin per stake rather than GGR, and that the 2026 World Cup / 2028 Euros cycle will set the acquisition cost curve — with illegal streaming and cloaked advertising competing for the same audience at the same moments.

segments.name: Online casino, poker & crypto
segments.headline: Casino is 70% of the EU27 online marketplace and the product where licensed operators are weakest (~24% channelisation by GCI's count); where it is banned or handicapped, the leak is structural.
narrative: Casino (including poker and crypto-denominated play) is the dominant online product: 70% of EU27 online GGR in 2025 (68% in 2024), implying ~€90.2bn (~$98.8bn) [derived]. It is 59% of regulated GGR (~€21.5bn, ~$23.5bn) but 75% of illegal GGR (~€68.7bn, ~$75.2bn), so by GCI's measure only about one euro in four of casino GGR is earned under a local licence. Unlicensed GGR is most casino-heavy in Western Europe (80%) and Northern Europe (78%) — the regions with the most restrictive or newest licensed casino regimes — and least in Southern Europe (69%).

H2/EGBA's series shows licensed-plus-grey online casino at €21.5bn (~$23.5bn) for EU27+UK in 2024 (45% of online GGR), up 14% from €18.9bn (~$20.7bn) in 2023, forecast at €23.2bn (~$25.4bn) for 2025 and compounding 7.5% to €30.8bn by 2029 — the fastest-growing product after online lottery. Online poker is flat at €1.5bn (~$1.6bn, 2.3% CAGR) and bingo/other €1.6bn. It is notable that H2's EU27+UK casino figure coincides with GCI's EU27-only regulated casino (~€21.5bn): either GCI's regulated casino is generous or H2's includes a sizeable UK and grey component — another reason to treat the product cut as indicative.

Country mixes reflect regulation as much as taste. EGBA's 2023 data show casino above 60% of online GGR in Malta (73%), Estonia (72%) and Latvia (63%); France and Cyprus prohibit online casino for licensed operators, so EGBA notes their small casino figures 'reflect fully offshore casino activity'. Poland reserves online casino to the state operator and Germany's GlüStV permits online slots and poker nationally under a €1 stake limit and 5.3% turnover tax, with table games left to the Länder [background, not re-verified this session]. Euromat identifies product bans in CY, FR, DE and PL and monopolies in AT, FI, HU, PL and SI as primary leakage drivers; GCI lists KYC, self-exclusion, age limits, responsible-gaming tooling, cross-sell limits and taxation as the frictions unlicensed casinos exploit, and adds 'product bleed' from prediction markets as a new vector.

The unlicensed casino ecosystem is professionalised. Euromat finds the 25 largest illegal brands account for ~64% of black-market traffic; GCI documents Stake's migration from Twitch (banned Oct 2022) to the Kick platform (launched Dec 2022 under common ownership), with Kick's slots category accessible in 21 of 27 member states and the six 'blocks' (BE, FR, GR, IT, MT, SK) effective only in Greece, while 26 of 27 states had affiliate advertising for unlicensed casinos on Kick. Unlicensed casinos explicitly market self-exclusion avoidance ('casinos not on CRUKS', 'not on ROFUS').

Commercially, casino is where licensed economics are most sensitive to the regulatory design. Markets opening full online casino under GGR taxation (Finland from 2027, Austria post-reform, Ireland under its new regime) are the genuine greenfield opportunities; Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands and Southern Europe are mature GGR-tax casino markets where share is won on product and CRM; France, Poland and Germany should not anchor a casino-led business case under current rules. Pricing and bonus intensity must assume an unlicensed competitor paying ~2% gaming tax and no KYC friction.

segments.name: Land-based, lottery & retail (EU27 + UK)
segments.headline: Retail is still 61% of European GGR (€75.5bn) and growing ~1.8% a year; lottery is the single largest product (€38bn) and the fastest-growing online vertical (7.7% CAGR) — but it sits behind state monopolies.
narrative: The EGBA/H2 series is the only consolidated view of the land-based market (GCI excludes it entirely). Total European GGR (EU27 plus UK) was €123.4bn (~$135.1bn) in 2024, up 5% on 2023, of which land-based contributed €75.5bn (~$82.7bn, 61%) and online €47.9bn (~$52.5bn, 39%); H2 forecasts €127.7bn (~$139.8bn) for 2025 with online crossing 40% at €51.1bn (~$56.0bn), and €149.2bn (~$163.4bn) by 2029 with online at 45%. Land-based is forecast to compound 1.8% a year to €82.4bn (~$90.2bn) by 2029 against 6.9% for online.

Within land-based, lottery is €30.9bn (~$33.8bn, 41% of retail GGR, +1.7% CAGR), gaming machines €24.9bn (~$27.3bn, 33%, +1.6%), casino €8.5bn (~$9.3bn, 11%, +2.5%), sports and events betting €6.4bn (~$7.0bn, 9%, +2.5%), horse racing €3.2bn (~$3.5bn) and bingo/other €1.6bn (~$1.8bn). Lottery is also the largest product overall at €38.0bn (~$41.6bn) once its €7.1bn (~$7.8bn) online component is added, and online lottery has the strongest growth outlook of any online vertical (7.7% CAGR to €10.4bn by 2029), strongest in Germany (37% of online GGR) and Denmark (26%).

Country structure is retail-heavy outside the Nordics and the UK. In 2023 Italy was Europe's largest market at €21.0bn (~$23.0bn) with only 21.7% online (€4.6bn, ~$5.0bn); the UK was €19.8bn (~$21.7bn) with €11.1bn (~$12.2bn, 56%) online; Germany €14.4bn (~$15.8bn, 22.6% online); France €14.0bn (~$15.3bn, 27% online, €3.8bn); Spain had the lowest online share at 14.2%. Sweden (68.3%), Finland and Denmark (68.1%) are the most digital, and 13 countries have online shares above 50%.

The constituency behind the headline report is itself land-based: the ECA represents licensed casinos and their online arms, chaired by the CEO of Casinos Austria and Austrian Lotteries, and Euromat represents the gaming-machine and amusement sector. Both are arguing for enforcement against the unlicensed online sector rather than for liberalisation, and the ECA explicitly opposes offsetting leakage by raising taxes on licensed operators. Lottery and most casino concessions remain state-owned or exclusive in every member state, and GCI's licensing timeline shows the EU's private online markets opened progressively (Malta 2004, Italy 2006, France 2010, Spain 2011, Denmark 2012, Portugal 2015, Sweden 2019, Germany/Netherlands 2021, Finland 2026+ and Austria 2027).

For an online-first operator the retail market matters in three ways: omnichannel is a share lever in Italy and Spain where retail still dominates and licences are often tied to concessions; lottery monopolies (FDJ, Veikkaus, Lotto, SISAL-type operators) are increasingly also licensed online competitors; and the land-based lobby is now the loudest voice on EU-level enforcement, which shapes the regulatory agenda far more than the online associations.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime (EU framework and national)
segments.headline: No EU gambling law and none coming: 27 national licences averaging €1.1m to enter and 24% of GGR to operate, versus €8k and 2.3% offshore — the cost asymmetry that the ECA says 'must not become an advantage for those who ignore the law'.
narrative: Gambling is regulated at member-state level. There is no EU sector directive; national regimes operate under the Treaty's free-movement rules as interpreted by the Court of Justice, which permits restrictions (monopolies, licence caps, product bans) where they are justified by consumer-protection or crime-prevention objectives and applied consistently and proportionately [background; the ECA notes the CJEU 'has confirmed this principle']. The ECA's position is explicit — 'national licences, European cooperation against criminals' — and it does not ask for an EU gaming law or regulator; EU-level leverage therefore runs through anti-money-laundering (gambling operators are obliged entities; the new Anti-Money Laundering Authority attended the ECA's July 2026 roundtable), Europol (the Commission has proposed reforming its mandate), Eurojust and platform rules rather than through gambling legislation. Malta's 2023 'Bill 55' shielding MGA licensees from foreign judgments is the live test of the limits of the Malta-licence model, with the Commission having opened legal action [headline only; not read in full this session].

GCI's 2025 benchmark quantifies the licensed-versus-transnational cost gap. The average initial multi-product licence fee across EU27 regimes is €1.1m (~$1.2m) against €8,183 (~$9.0k) at Anjouan, Curaçao, the Isle of Man and Malta; average recurring fees are €355k (~$389k) against €33k (~$36k) where recurring regimes exist; average gaming tax is 24.0% of GGR against 2.3%; and average corporate tax is 18.9% against 8.8%. EU regulators additionally require bank guarantees and share capital that transnational licensors (Malta excepted) do not. GCI stresses that Malta is simultaneously an EU member and a transnational licensor, and that a transnational licence 'does not provide authorization to operate in every jurisdiction' — the 'there is no grey market' doctrine the ECA has adopted.

Tax bases differ and are moving up. Most member states tax online GGR (the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Spain, Italy, Belgium, Greece, Romania, the Baltics, Malta, Finland's new regime), while Germany, Poland and Ireland tax betting stakes and Portugal taxes sports-betting turnover [background list, not re-verified this session]. Recent increases include the Netherlands (30.5% to 34.2% in 2025 and 37.8% from 2026) and Sweden (18% to 22% from July 2024) [background]. A BGC-commissioned H2GC study forecasts an 11ppt fall in Dutch channelisation after the 2025 increase and reports that the Dutch regulator itself forecast tax receipts down 9% in 2025 versus 2024; the KSA's spring report described licensed Dutch gambling as stagnating while the black market grows. Euromat identifies consumer-price taxation in AT, HR, DE, IE, PL and PT as a leakage driver, and the ECA warns that 'every additional burden placed on legal operators strengthens the position of illegal operators'.

Licensing timelines show a two-decade opening that is not yet complete. Malta regulated remote gaming in 2004, Italy 2006, France 2010 (betting, horse racing, poker only), Spain 2011, Denmark and Schleswig-Holstein 2012, Portugal 2015, Sweden 2019, Germany (Interstate Treaty) and the Netherlands (KOA) 2021. Finland is replacing the Veikkaus monopoly with private licensing (go-live 2027), Austria's government approved a reform to open the online market on 25 Nov 2026 ahead of its licences expiring in 2027, and Ireland's new regulator published a draft list of licensable games this week. Hungary, Poland (casino) and Slovenia retain monopoly or near-monopoly structures. No consolidated EU licence register exists: EGBA's nine members hold 401 online licences across 22 jurisdictions; total licensee counts per state were not verifiable in-session (n/a).

Country-level rates in the table below are background reference points carried from prior research and flagged '†' — they were not re-verified against the regulators in this session because the research tool budget was exhausted, and should be confirmed with the ADM, DGOJ, ANJ, GGL, KSA, Spelinspektionen, Spillemyndigheden, SRIJ and HGC before use. The strategic conclusion does not depend on them: multi-market EU entry costs roughly €1m-plus per licence, 20–40% of GGR in tax, 12–24 months of application lead time and a separate compliance stack per state, and there is no credible route to serve EU consumers lawfully from a single transnational licence.

segments.name: Payments, advertising, responsible gambling & enforcement ecosystem
segments.headline: Licensed operators carry the AML, RG and advertising burden while the unlicensed sector buys 85%-approved cloaked ads, streams to 17.8bn World Cup views and markets 'not on CRUKS' — the policy answer now forming is payments and platform enforcement, not more rules for licensees.
narrative: Payments are the lever both trade bodies now prioritise. The ECA's chairman argues that if banks, card schemes and 'all payment services stopped transferring money to illegal operators, their business model would break'; GCI's 'ecosystem essentials' model treats payment providers as enabling deposits at scale and describes transnational licensing as delivering 'banking continuity' and 'payment-processing coverage and resilience' through a 'triangle trade' that separates licensing, sites/apps and content across jurisdictions so there is no single point of failure. Crypto-funded play is included in GCI's unlicensed estimate (Stake is its principal case study). No payment-method mix for the EU27 is disclosed by any source read (n/a); several member states already hold statutory payment-blocking powers [background, not re-verified], but GCI's data on 6,238 transacting destinations implies they are not biting.

Advertising is where the asymmetry is most visible. Licensed advertising is heavily restricted in roughly 46% of the 28 markets Euromat studied (BE, BG, HR, CY, DE, IT, LV, LT, NL, PL, RO, ES among them), while GCI found cloaked-advertising brokers — more than half of them EU-based — openly selling campaigns into every EU27 state with an average 85% platform-approval rate, 3x advertised return on ad spend and 1,100-plus promised first-time depositors a month, principally through Google and Meta. Affiliate numbers promoting unlicensed operators fell from 21,106 (2023) to 17,501 (2025) even as unlicensed GGR rose, which GCI reads as consolidation into larger affiliates. AI search assistants that recommend operators without checking local licensing are flagged as a new discovery channel, and the ECA has called on search engines and AI providers to perform licensing due diligence.

Responsible-gambling architecture is being weaponised by the unlicensed sector. National self-exclusion registers (CRUKS in the Netherlands, ROFUS in Denmark) are used as search hooks — 'casinos not on CRUKS' — and GCI notes that for self-excluded and underage users unlicensed sites may be 'the only accessible gambling options', outside age verification, dispute resolution and deposit controls. Population impact reached 23.03% of EU27 residents in 2025 (29.26% in Eastern Europe), with 16.76% reached by unlicensed content; audience exposure was 91% unlicensed. Streaming platforms compound this: Kick's slots category is nominally blocked in six member states but functionally in one, and 26 of 27 states carried unlicensed affiliate advertising on Kick.

Enforcement remains national while the activity is cross-border. The ECA's July 2026 roundtable in the European Parliament (MEP Lukas Mandl; Commission, AMLA, Eurojust, the Europol JPSG and national regulators attending) called for stronger enforcement and cooperation, timed to the Commission's proposal to reform Europol's mandate; the ECA's November asks are regulator–police–FIU information sharing, coordinated payment and advertising disruption, and platform/app-store/search take-downs; Euromat is calling for a European taskforce; GCI proposes a 'Monitor, Police, Enforce, Optimize' cycle across the whole marketplace rather than licensee-only supervision. The ECA explicitly warns governments not to respond by raising taxes on licensees.

For B2Tech the implications are operational and budgetary: expect AML obligations to tighten (AMLA operational from 2027 [background]), advertising rules to stay restrictive in the large Western and Southern markets, and self-exclusion, deposit-limit and affordability tooling to be table stakes in every licence application. The upside is that the enforcement consensus is finally pointing at payments, platforms and affiliates — the channels that most directly determine licensed operators' acquisition costs — but the timeline to measurable channelisation gains is years, not quarters.

highlights.text: Licensed online demand is compounding: EU27 regulated online GGR €36.5bn (~$40.0bn) in 2025, +8.6% after +30% in 2024 (GCI), with H2 showing the licensed EU online market +11% in 2025 and EGBA's nine members +34% to €18.0bn (~$19.7bn) — scale incumbents are gaining share inside the licensed pool.

Three greenfield licensed markets open inside 24 months: Finland (monopoly to licensing, go-live 2027), Austria (government approved reform on 25 Nov 2026; licences expire 2027) and Ireland (new GRAI regime, draft eligible-game list published this week) — all are casino-inclusive, GGR-tax regimes where there is no entrenched licensed competitor base.

Casino is 70% of the EU27 online marketplace and the fastest-growing licensed product (H2: online casino 7.5% CAGR to €30.8bn (~$33.7bn) by 2029 for EU27+UK); where regulation allows a full casino product, the addressable pool is largest.

Sports betting is the better-channelised product (~40% licensed by GCI's count vs ~24% for casino) and the 2026 World Cup / 2028 Euros cycle provides acquisition peaks; the illegal-growth deceleration to +13.6% in 2025 may partly reverse in 2026 but licensed operators also benefit from tournament demand.

Northern (42% regulated) and Southern Europe (40%; regulated GGR +12% in 2025 to €11.3bn, ~$12.4bn) offer the best channelisation and GGR-based tax regimes — the lowest-risk entry points for a multi-market build.

The enforcement consensus (ECA, Euromat, GCI, Commission/Europol/AMLA engagement) has shifted to payments, platforms, app stores, search/AI and affiliates — the channels that set licensed operators' acquisition costs; any effective action lifts licensed channelisation without new costs to licensees.

Transnational-licence arbitrage is being closed politically ('there is no grey market'), with Malta's Bill 55 under EU legal action — a durable advantage for operators that invest in local licences over those running 'dot-com' models into the EU.

lowlights.text: Tax creep on licensees: average EU27 gaming tax 24% of GGR (GCI) with recent rises in the Netherlands (37.8% from 2026) and Sweden (22%) [background]; H2GC forecasts an 11ppt channelisation decline in the Netherlands after the 2025 rise and the KSA itself forecast tax receipts −9% — governments facing €22.9bn (~$25.1bn) of claimed 'lost' tax may be tempted to raise rates further on the operators they can reach.

Entry and compliance costs are high and non-portable: average initial multi-product licence fee €1.1m (~$1.2m), recurring €355k (~$389k), plus bank guarantees/share capital, 27 separate regimes, no passporting and separate AML/RG/advertising stacks per state; transnational licences cost €8,183 (~$9.0k) but confer no EU authorisation.

The size of the illegal competitor set is contested by 5–8x (GCI €91.6bn/72% vs H2 ~€18bn/27% vs Euromat ~€12bn net/25%); GCI's methodology (audience-based value-per-visit, every transacting domain incl. mirrors, crypto included) is proprietary and industry-commissioned, so policy — and any business case — rests on numbers that cannot be independently reconciled.

Advertising restrictions are 'significant' in ~46% of markets (Euromat: BE, BG, HR, CY, DE, IT, LV, LT, NL, PL, RO, ES) while unlicensed operators buy cloaked ads with 85% approval and 3x ROAS and reach 91% of engaged audiences — licensed CAC is structurally higher in exactly the largest markets.

Product bans and monopolies cap the legal offer in major markets: online casino prohibited for licensees in France and Cyprus, state monopoly in Poland, restricted slots/poker-only with €1 stake caps and 5.3% turnover tax in Germany [background], monopolies in Hungary and Slovenia — Eastern Europe is 81% unlicensed and Western Europe 74%.

Illegal-market growth remains double-digit (+13.6% to €91.6bn, ~$100.3bn in 2025) with the operator count flat at ~6,200 — i.e. the surviving unlicensed brands are getting bigger and more professional (25 brands ≈64% of traffic per Euromat), and illegal streaming of the 2026 World Cup (17.8bn views, 95% with unlicensed ads) shows the recruitment engine is intact.

Headline figures carry internal inconsistencies — 2025 tax loss €22.9bn (ECA) vs €22.0bn (GCI/CFG), total €128.0bn vs €128.1bn — and the land-based constituency behind the report has an interest in portraying online leakage as maximal; treat the numbers as advocacy-grade, not regulator-grade.

forecast.intro: The bridge from the 2023 baseline to the 2025 release is a marketplace that grew €49.7bn (~$54.4bn) in annual GGR, of which licensed operators kept €10.7bn (~$11.7bn) and the unlicensed sector €39.0bn (~$42.7bn) by GCI's count; the regulated base moved from €25.8bn to €36.5bn (~$40.0bn) and its share from 33% to 28%. The moving parts for 2026–28 are (i) three market openings (Finland 2027, Austria post-2027 licence expiry, Ireland's GRAI regime), (ii) continued tax escalation in mature markets (Netherlands 37.8% from 2026, Sweden 22%) that H2GC expects to cost channelisation, (iii) an EU-level enforcement pivot toward payments, platforms, affiliates and search/AI via Europol, AMLA and platform rules rather than a gambling directive, and (iv) the contested black-market denominator, where the policy narrative (72% illegal) is far more aggressive than the industry-standard series (25–27%).

bridge.title: Illegal online GGR 2025 — GCI vs competing estimates

forecast.view: Our independent view: the licensed EU27 online pool should reach roughly **€39–41bn (~$43–45bn) in 2026 and €42–45bn (~$46–49bn) in 2027** (estimate; +8–10% a year, in line with H2's 6.9% EU27+UK CAGR plus the Finnish, Austrian and Irish openings), with **online casino compounding faster than sports** and online lottery the quiet outperformer. We do not expect licensed share to recover on GCI's measure within two years — enforcement against payments and platforms will take time to bite and the 2026 World Cup will have re-accelerated illegal acquisition — but we also think **the 72% figure overstates the economic black market**; for planning we would assume an unlicensed competitor set of 25–35% of online GGR in well-regulated Northern/Southern markets and 50%+ in Eastern Europe and product-restricted Western markets. **Tax direction is up, not down**: governments will read €22.9bn of 'lost' tax as a reason to extract more from licensees rather than to lower rates, so model 2–4pp of GGR-tax creep in mature markets by 2028 and margin compression where turnover taxes persist. **Regulatory direction is national licensing plus EU-level enforcement**: expect AMLA-driven AML tightening from 2027, DSA/platform pressure on Kick, Meta and Google, payment-blocking expansion, and continued legal attrition of the Malta 'dot-com' model — all of which raise the relative value of holding local licences. Leverage for an entrant is therefore in timing (apply early for FI/AT/IE), product (full casino under GGR tax), and operating cost (shared compliance stack across 5–8 GGR-tax markets rather than a 27-state footprint).
watch: Finland: licence application window, go-live on 1 Jan 2027 and the final tax rate and RG rules for private operators
Austria: passage of the November 2026 reform through parliament, licence tender timetable ahead of the 2027 expiry, and whether a GGR tax replaces the 40% monopoly levy
Ireland: GRAI licence categories, fees and timing of the first licensing windows after the draft eligible-games list
Netherlands: 2026 channelisation and tax-take data under the 37.8% rate as the live test of the tax-versus-leakage trade-off
EU enforcement: Europol mandate reform, AMLA's first supervisory actions against gambling PSPs/operators, and any Commission or CJEU outcome on Malta's Bill 55
Platform action: whether Kick/Stake, cloaked-ad brokers and AI search assistants are addressed under platform rules, and any EU-level payment-blocking coordination
Next GCI/ECA data (2026 edition, mid-2027) and the Euromat/H2 updates — specifically whether the illegal-growth deceleration (+13.6% in 2025) held through the 2026 World Cup
Germany's GlüStV evaluation and France's periodic online-casino debate — the two largest product-restricted Western markets where any opening would move the regulated pool by billions

report.confidenceNote: FX: EUR/USD 1.095 as of 25 Nov 2026, inferred from contemporaneous press conversions of the release (iGB €91.6bn = $100.1bn; Yogonet €224.8bn = $246.15bn); all '~$' figures are at this rate. Headline market-size and illegal-market figures are from an industry-commissioned (ECA) study by GCI using a proprietary audience/'value-per-visit' methodology; they are not regulator statistics, and the two competing estimates (Euromat/Regulus-Helios ~€12bn net, ~25%; H2 ~€18bn, ~27%) differ by 5–8x — confidence in the illegal-market figures is LOW, in the regulated base (corroborated by EGBA/H2 and IMGL) MEDIUM-HIGH. Internal inconsistencies flagged: 2025 tax loss €22.9bn (ECA, Jul/Nov 2026) vs €22.0bn (GCI/CFG, Sept 2026); 2025 total €128.0bn vs €128.1bn. Product-level euro values are derived by applying GCI's percentage splits to its totals. EGBA/H2 figures cover EU27 + UK and include grey-market online activity; 2024 is provisional and 2025 estimated. The research-tool budget was exhausted before national regulator datasets (ADM, DGOJ, ANJ, GGL, KSA, Spelinspektionen, Spillemyndigheden, SRIJ, HGC) could be fetched, so country-level tax rates, licence fees and policy details marked '†'/[background]/[unverified] are carried from prior knowledge and must be confirmed before use; the Austria reform, Ireland draft and Malta Bill 55 action were seen as headlines only. EU-wide licensed-operator counts and payment-method mix: n/a.
